Key true for one substance at one temperature; 'full one' and 'few spoonfuls' are the heat-versus-temperature confusion (M1), 'heated longer' the heating-time one (M4). No stem clause rules a choice out; T2 particles-in-motion never teaches temperature as an average, so it is this grade's fact. Voice clean.

Expansion is greater average spacing (Grokipedia); swollen particles is a listed misconception (MOSART); caloric filling the spaces is the late-1700s theory, obsolete by the 1850s; added matter is wrong. c08bde277d.why: Old tell fixed: 'slowly dries' is gone, and two choices are now about particles escaping, so the student has to know which ones leave and that temperature is their average. Key matches Grokipedia (the most energetic molecules escape and the rest cools). The wet bulb in moving air reads lower unless the air is saturated, and the pair is a psychrometer. 'Give off cold' and 'shield' are honest misconceptions. A 7th-grade particle explanation.

feb8d1e619.why: Looked at closely; it holds. Facts: solid particles vibrate all the time and that motion is thermal energy (Illinois Physics Van; Grokipedia: a frozen lake holds thermal energy); lab ULT freezers run at -80 to -86 C, far below a home freezer; 'only warm or hot objects have thermal energy' and 'cold is a substance' are MOSART misconceptions. Grade: the key's reason (ice particles still vibrate) is T2 particles-in-motion's answer, and T2 knowledge removes 'frozen still', as T1's 'cold never flows' removes 'soaked up cold'. But 'No, since only warm things hold it' stays live, and T1 energy-changes-form's 'a warm stone holds thermal energy' feeds it. Only this unit's own T3 idea, that thermal energy is the energy of the particles' motion even in a cold thing, settles it. Two Yes and two No choices; the stem's 'far colder' and 'at all' build the expectation the answer breaks; the stem names nothing; voice clean. Close to T2, not a re-ask.
